paper_title: Solv3R: 3D Looped Transformer as a Multi-view Solver

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Classical structure-from-motion reconstruction proceeds iteratively, refining camera poses and scene geometry from a current estimate. This allows maps to easily expand without recomputing already computed views, or geometry estimates to improve as more observations are provided. Most geometric foundation models, however, predict entire geometry in a single forward pass or update a recurrent state as frames arrive sequentially, making this expansion and refinement non-trivial. We introduce Solv3R, a looped transformer that learns to continue solving multi-view geometry from its current state. Importantly, its update operator is independent of the iteration count, allowing previously refined and newly introduced views to be jointly updated regardless of how ``solved'' they are. We train the operator to preserve accurate reconstructions under continued iteration and correct inaccurate states, enabling refinement of fixed image collections and integration of new observations. Representations of solved views can also be cached once and reused as geometric context across iterations, enabling compact and efficient key-value caching. We analyze the solver dynamics and compare it with the state-of-the-art, demonstrating that a single learned solver supports offline reconstruction, incremental reconstruction, relocalization, and streaming without task-specific training or modules. The code and models will be made publicly available at https://ubc-vision.github.io/solv3r/.

Teaser. We present Solv3R, looped transformer that learns to solve multi-view geometry from its current state. Diverse reconstruction settings, e.g., offline, incremental, online, and out-of-order reconstruction, can all be handled by our single learned solver.

sections.content: Classical structure-from-motion reconstruction proceeds iteratively, refining camera poses and scene geometry from current estimate. Most geometric foundation models, however, predict entire geometry in single forward pass or update recurrent state as frames arrive sequentially, making this expansion and refinement non-trivial. Representations of solved views can also be cached once and reused as geometric context across iterations, enabling compact and efficient key-value caching. The code and models will be made publicly available at https://ubc-vision.github.io/solv3r/. 1. Introduction Recent geometric foundation models (GFMs) [47, 51, 88, 89, 93, 95, 101] have driven shift in multi-view 3D 1 Figure 2. Comparison of geometric update mechanisms. Conventional GFMs [51, 88, 95] use successive layer-specific transformations, tying their intermediate representations to layer depth. Recurrent-memory models [21, 90] process incoming frames while updating persistent scene memory across observations. Although Dej`aView [12] shares transformer weights, its updates remain conditioned on the refinement step. Solv3R applies the same stationary update operator regardless of the iteration count, allowing previously refined and newly introduced views to be jointly updated. reconstruction toward predicting scene geometry directly from multi-view images. Unlike classical Structure-fromMotion (SfM), which relies on correspondence matching and iterative geometric optimization [69], these models estimate geometry in feed-forward manner. They typically employ successive transformer blocks to progressively build geometry-aware representations and predict camera poses, depths, and point maps. But large-scale reconstruction often extends beyond single forward pass. The image collection may exceed transformers input capacity, or new views may arrive after the initial reconstruction, such as subsequent video frames or additional images and videos of the same scene. Incorporating these views with feed-forward GFM typically requires processing the combined image set again [88, 95]. Streaming models [21, 45, 86, 90, 117] avoid this by updating state frame by frame, but they are limited to views that arrive sequentially. In contrast, classic SfM incorporates new observations into an existing reconstruction and uses iterative optimization to refine its estimates [69]. Hence, learned reconstruction model should likewise be able to continue solving from its current state, refining existing estimates and integrating new views as they arrive. This requires reconstruction state that remains usable for further geometric computation beyond the initial forward pass. But conventional feed-forward GFMs like VGGT [88] process image representations through successive transformer layers, each applying different learned transformation  (Fig. 2)  . Their intermediate states (i.e. tokens) are consequently tied to particular stages of computation (i.e. layer depth). Dej`aView [12] moves toward iterative reconstruction by repeatedly applying shared transformer block. However, its architecture remains conditioned on the refinement step, allowing the same block to perform different transformations at different stages. In contrast, classical stationary iterative solver such as Jacobi [10], applies the same update at every iteration, and does not need to know which iteration it is operating on. It can thus continue from any state, including one whose variables have received different numbers of iterations. key observation is that sharing weights alone does not give Dej`aView this ability. We thus posit that GFM should be learning-based multi-view solver. Given more computation, solver should continue refining reconstruction until convergence, and once converged, the solution should not change with further iterations. solver of this type should handle offline reconstruction, adding views, and streaming with one unifying architecture (see Fig. 1). To this end, we introduce Solv3R, an architecture that reformulates multi-view reconstruction as reusable learning-based geometric solver. Solv3R employs stationary (i.e. timestep invariant) learned geometric update operator that acts on the current multi-view state. We train this operator so that solved reconstruction stays unchanged under further iterations, and so that reconstruction with errors, for example one with newly added views, converges to the solution  (Fig. 3)  . With these solver properties, Solv3R unifies different reconstruction settings through single learned geometric solving process. Our solver achieves competitive accuracy in conventional multi-view reconstruction, while allowing existing estimates to be jointly revised as new observations arrive. This reuse extends beyond reconstruction states to attention context: fixed reconstructed map can provide single KV cache reused across solver calls. Together, these capabilities support incremental reconstruction, map-based relocalization, and streaming reconstruction without taskspecific learned modules, achieving competitive streaming performance even without streaming-specific training. Through extensive analyses of solver dynamics and experiments across reconstruction scenarios, we demonstrate how reusable geometric computation enables flexible and efficient multi-view reconstruction. 2 ing separate learned reconstruction process for streaming, Solv3R applies the same geometric solver to both offline and online reconstruction. 3. Method Our key idea is to make the shared block of looped transformer act as the iteration of classical solver, whose update logic does not depend on how many iterations have already run. We review looped transformers for 3D reconstruction in Sec. 3.1, and use simple classical solver in Sec. 3.2 to define the properties that we want from such solver. We then replace the classical iteration with learned operator in Sec. 3.3, and discuss its properties in Sec. 3.4. 3.1. Looped transformers for 3D reconstruction Dej`aView [12] formulates multi-view reconstruction as iterative refinement of latent state. Given input images I={Ii}N i=1, an image encoder initializes multi-view state z0, which is repeatedly updated by shared transformer block with frame-wise and global attention. The refined state is decoded into depth and ray maps, from which scene geometry and camera poses are recovered. Unlike conventional feed-forward transformers with independently parameterized layers, Dej`aView shares the transformer block across iterations, but conditions each update on the step: zk+1 = Fθ(zk; τk), (1) where τk is the conditioning on the iteration index k, which lets the shared block apply different transformation at each iteration. Because of this structure, Dej`aView loses reconstruction accuracy when iterated beyond its trained range, as we demonstrate in Section 4. More fundamentally, each state is tied to the iteration index at which it was computed. One application of Fθ thus cannot jointly update views that have received different numbers of iterations, because no single τk matches all of them. Thus, sharing weights alone does not give the block an update that is independent of the iteration index. 3.2. An iterative solver as running example To make the properties we want concrete, consider classical constraint satisfaction problem, solving linear system Ax=b with the Jacobi method [10]. The rows of matrix and corresponding observations define the constraints, and the state holds the current estimate of the unknowns. Starting from an initial state x0, each iteration applies the same update: xk+1 = Φ(xk; A, b), (2) We call one iteration, that is, one application of Φ, solver call. The update Φ does not depend on the iteration index k, which makes the Jacobi stationary [10]. When the method converges, three properties follow: Figure 3. Continuing geometric solving with new observations. When new views are introduced, Solv3R continues solving from its existing state, jointly refining both previously reconstructed and newly added views. Dej`aView struggles to maintain consistent reconstruction. Numbers indicate camera rotation errors in degrees. 2. Related work Geometric foundation models (GFMs) have advanced feedforward 3D reconstruction, progressing from pairwise pointmap regression and matching [47, 93] to joint prediction of camera poses and dense geometry from multiple views [15, 28, 51, 75, 88, 95, 101]. Recent methods further improve multi-view geometric prediction and scalability [19, 20, 3032, 63, 87, 89, 99, 114]. Related advances extend geometric prediction to monocular inputs [35, 91, 92, 102], incorporate additional geometric priors [38, 42, 56, 58, 65], or produce renderable Gaussian representations [22, 100, 105, 106]. Learned iterative refinement and solvers. Learned iterative refinement has been widely applied to optical flow, stereo, multi-view depth, and visual SLAM [8, 41, 53, 77, 78, 85, 112]. Related work on equilibrium and recurrent models investigates fixed-point behavior, stability, and extended computation [1, 7, 9, 29]. Inspired by recent advances in looped transformers for language models [5, 6, 24, 34, 39, 61, 103, 115, 116], Dej`aView [12] introduces shared recurrent computation for multi-view reconstruction. We extend this direction to continued geometric solving across fixed and evolving view sets, including views at different refinement stages. Continuous and streaming 3D reconstruction. Continuous reconstruction methods maintain and update geometric information as new observations arrive. Some approaches employ persistent scene representations or test-time adaptation [21, 86, 90, 98, 113], while others preserve geometric context through causal attention and caching [18, 45, 108, 117]. Window-based methods further integrate local reconstructions through registration and optimization [26, 50, 54, 55, 59, 62, 109, 111]. Rather than introduc3 Figure 4. Overview. Left: stationary transformer block repeatedly updates the multi-view state through frame-wise and global attention, initial-state injection, and state normalization. Right: The same operator continues refining the reconstruction across solver calls, allowing new views to be introduced at any stage and jointly updated with existing views. Camera poses, depth maps, and ray maps can be decoded from the current state after any solver call. (P1) Stability. The accurate solution x, which satisfies Ax=b, is fixed point with Φ(x; A, b)=x, so further solver calls leave it unchanged. (P2) Correction. Consider perturbed state, that is, solution moved off by, for example, added noise. From such state, the same solver calls converge back to x. (P3) Continuation. When new unknowns and constraints are added, the solver can start the old unknowns from their solved values, and the new ones from an initial guess. It then updates all of them together toward the solution of the enlarged system, often in fewer solver calls than restart from x0. The state holds values that have received different numbers of solver calls, and Φ still updates them in one solver call. It can do so because it does not depend on how state was reached. Multi-view reconstruction has the same structure. The input images define the constraints, the per-view states hold the current estimate, and the cameras and depths decoded from the state are the current estimate of the solution. solved state is one whose decoded cameras and depths are accurate, and which further solver calls change little. learned multi-view solver should thus leave solved reconstruction unchanged under further solver calls (P1), correct perturbed reconstruction (P2), and continue from solved reconstruction when views are added (P3). Like Φ, time independent). It needs neither the iteration index nor the number of solver calls that each view has received. The state may thus combine views with different numbers of solver calls, zk=(z[h1] ), where view has received hi calls. We inject z0 at every solver call for the same reason that Φ reads and at every call. The state tracks the current estimate, while z0 carries the constraints from the images. Attention infers how the views constrain each other. Without z0, each call would see only the current state, and errors in the state could accumulate over calls. We instantiate Tθ as single transformer block that is completely shared across solver calls, with frame-wise and global attention. We this fine-tune from the pretrained block Dej`aView [12], and make its update stationary with two changes. First, Dej`aView scales the channels of each sub-block with gates computed from the conditioning τk on the iteration index. We replace these gates with learned constant gates, which apply the same channel-wise scaling at every solver call. Second, to keep the magnitude of the state from drifting over many solver calls, we rescale the updated state to fixed root-mean-square (RMS) norm. We use single scale factor for the whole state, which preserves the relative magnitudes across views. Stationarity alone does not make Tθ converge. We thus train it to satisfy P1P3, as detailed in Sec. 3.4. Figure 5. Stable and corrective solver dynamics. Left: pose accuracy and relative state update norm over solver calls. Dej`aView is trained with up to 16 steps (shaded). Middle: camera rotation error and relative state update aligned to the solver call at which each window meets the stopping criterion of (5), showing median and interquartile range. Right: rotation error at call 16 after perturbations at call 8 using relative (rel.) or fixed-scale (fixed) Gaussian noise, or state resets (reset). 3.4. Learning solver dynamics We train Tθ to satisfy P1P3. When the input images do not change, solved state should change little under further solver calls, Tθ(z; z0)z. From perturbed state, the same operator should bring the reconstruction back to the solution. We thus train it on states that have received different numbers of solver calls, as well as on perturbed states. Training states. To keep solved states unchanged under further solver calls (P1), we train the operator on heterogeneous states. In the main training stage, starting from z0, we apply random number of solver calls without gradients, followed by several differentiable calls with supervision at the final call. This exposes the operator to states at different refinement stages, encouraging stable updates under continued computation. To train the operator to correct perturbed states (P2), we occasionally perturb the state before the differentiable callswe either add Gaussian noise to the whole state or reset subset of views to z0. Gaussian noise mimics deviations from solution, while partial resets simulate newly introduced views alongside refined ones (P3). Similar in spirit to denoising-based learning [72, 83] and Diffusion Forcing [17], these perturbations expose the operator to broader range of states, encouraging corrective refinement beyond its usual trajectories. Geometric supervision. We supervise geometric predictions after varying numbers of solver calls, rather than after fixed number. At the end of each sampled rollout, we decode camera poses, ray maps, and depths from the current state and apply ground-truth geometric supervision where available. We do not supervise the states of earlier calls; instead, varying the supervised call trains the operator to produce accurate geometry at any call between the 24th and the 48th. To preserve the priors of the pretrained Dej`aView, we also distill its predictions after 16 solver calls into the solver.

Experiments We initialize from the pretrained looped transformer [12] and fine-tune using AdamW [57] with learning rate of 2105 and an exponential moving average (EMA) of the weights. Offline reconstruction We first compare our method with state-of-the-art multiview reconstruction methods on standard benchmarks. As shown in Table 1, Solv3R achieves competitive camera pose and geometry accuracy with compact model. Importantly, Solv3R retains accuracy comparable to Dej`aView at the same 16-call budget while exhibiting the stable and corrective solver dynamics demonstrated in Section 4. These properties enable continued refinement and reuse of previously computed states beyond predefined iteration schedule. The stable solver dynamics also enable adaptive inference using (5), with γ=0.02 and maximum of 64 solver calls. With adaptive stopping, we can improve nearly all reconstruction metrics over our fixed-budget inference with only 34 additional solver calls on average. 5.2. Incremental reconstruction We next evaluate whether Solv3R can extend and revise an existing reconstruction as new observations arrive. Using evaluation windows from DL3DV [52] and ScanNet++ [107], we first solve four views for eight calls, introduce twelve additional views, and continue joint refinement from the existing states. As shown in Figure 8, Solv3R reconstructs the new views while improving the camera estimates of the original views, whereas Dej`aView fails to maintain consistent reconstruction. Compared with the no-join control using the same number of solver calls, this improvement shows that new observations contribute to correcting the existing solution rather than merely benefiting from further computation. In Figure 9, we examine revisability across different refinement stages and the efficiency of reusing previous computation. Adding new views at different refinement stages, even after the initial reconstruction meets the stopping criterion, improves original-view accuracy in most evaluation windows. When incrementally expanding the reconstruction from 8 to 64 views, Solv3R achieves accuracy comparable to re-solving from scratch with fewer solver calls and lower total runtime. These results show that existing reconstructions can be revised as new observations arrive while reusing previous computation, rather than repeatedly solving from scratch. 5.3. Implementation details We provide details of the architecture, training, and streaming configuration of Solv3R. Architecture. We build on the pretrained Dej`aView [12], retaining its shared transformer block with frame-wise and global attention. We replace the step-conditioned gates with learnable constant gates, which provide the same channelwise scaling in each sub-block across all solver calls. We initialize these gates by averaging the corresponding gate values over the 16 refinement steps of Dej`aView. To keep the state grounded in the original observations and stable under continued computation, we inject the initial state at every solver call and normalize the updated state: = Uθ(zk + z0), zk+1 = ρ uRMS . (6) Here, zk is the state after solver calls, Uθ denotes the shared block, z0 is the layer-normalized [4] initial state without affine parameters, and is zero-initialized linear projection. The target RMS ρ is the RMS of the final Dej`aView state, measured once before training (ρ 0.85), and stays fixed throughout training and inference. We scale the entire state by single factor, which preserves relative feature magnitudes across views and tokens. The resulting model has 117M parameters. It takes images whose longer side is 504 pixels. Training data. To cover diverse scenes, we train on broad mixture of indoor, object-centric, outdoor, driving, and synthetic datasets, summarized in Table 5. Training objective. The geometric loss Lgeo supervises the ray maps, cameras, and depths decoded at the final call. For ray maps, we apply an L1 loss to ray directions and scale-aligned ray origins. For cameras, we use geodesic losses on the relative rotations and translation directions. For depth, we use scale-aligned log-L1 loss with weight 0.5. On datasets with dense and accurate depth, we add multi-scale depth-gradient loss [49] with weight 0.5. These terms align each prediction to the ground truth with its own scale. They do not enforce common scale across views or between depths and camera translations, so we add two consistency terms with weight 1.5 each. The first penalizes the deviation of each views depth scale from the window mean. The second supervises the camera centers and ray origins after rescaling them by the windows depth scale. The distillation loss Ldist applies the ray, log-depth, and camera losses against the 16-step predictions of Dej`aView, with λdist = 0.5. For datasets whose ground truth is sparse or noisy, marked with in Table 5, we use Ldist only. Training procedure. For each incoming frame, the solver operates on window of anchors, memory frames, recent frames, and the new frame. The first frames serve as anchors that fix the coordinate frame and are initially solved jointly for 16 calls. The most recent frames form the active window, where each new frame is initialized from its image encoding plus the solved offset of the previous frame. Evaluation protocols We detail the evaluation protocols for the solver-property analyses and the offline, incremental, map-based relocalization, and streaming experiments. Solver properties. The stability analysis of the main paper uses 148 eight-view windows, 66 from DTU [40], 37 from ETH3D [70], and 45 from ScanNet++ [107] scenes held out from our fine-tuning. We measure rotation errors relative to the first view of each window. To test recovery, we perturb the state of 36 of these windows, 12 from each dataset, at call 8 and report the rotation error at call 16. Relative noise (rel.) is Gaussian noise with standard deviation of one or two times the RMS of the state of each model. Fixedscale noise (fixed) uses the mean state RMS of Solv3R and Dej`aView instead, so that both models receive the same absolute noise. reset returns every view except the first to its initial state. The other solver-property experiments use 64-frame sequences from the DL3DV [52] validation split and the held-out ScanNet++ scenes. Warm start simulates video that arrives one frame at time. The window holds the first frame, which fixes the coordinate frame, and the 23 most recent frames. When new frame arrives, the frames that stay in the window keep their solved states. The new frame starts from its initial state plus the solved offset of the previous frame, as in streaming (Sec. A). Over 16 sequences from each dataset, we count the solver calls until the rotation error of the new frame falls below 2, and compare them with solving the window from scratch. Pipelined reconstruction slides window of the first frame and the 16 most recent frames over sequence. It advances the window after every solver call rather than after convergence. After each call, the oldest frame other than the first leaves the window, and the next frame enters from its initial state. Apart from the first frame, each call thus updates frames that have received between 0 and 15 previous calls. We evaluate the pose of each frame when it leaves the window, after its 16th call. Random computational histories test whether the joint update depends on how each view reached its current state. We record the states of window over its first 16 calls from scratch, and build new state by taking each view from randomly chosen call of this trajectory. We then run 16 joint calls from this state, and report the mean difference of the camera rotations across 20 such draws for each of 96 windows of 16 views. Offline reconstruction. We follow the evaluation protocol and splits of Dej`aView [12] on DTU [40], ETH3D [70], 7-Scenes [71], ScanNet++ [107], and nuScenes [16]. We report the area under the curve (AUC) of relative pose errors at 3 and 30, and the relative L2 error and inlier ratio of the world-frame point maps. For adaptive inference, we stop when the relative update falls below γ = 0.02, with at least 4 and at most 64 solver calls. Without adaptive stopping, Solv3R runs 16 solver calls, the budget of Dej`aView. Incremental reconstruction. We use 20 scenes, 10 from the DL3DV validation split and 10 from the held-out ScanNet++ scenes. Starting from 8 views in capture order, we add 8 views at time up to 64 views, and report the pose AUC@10 over all view pairs after each insertion. Map-based relocalization. For each scene, we solve the training frames once as map and cache the key-value (KV) pairs of every map frame. Each test frame is query that we solve for 16 calls against cached map frames only. The attended frames are its 10 nearest map frames retrieved by NetVLAD [2], the reference view of the map, and 64 evenly spaced map frames that cover the scene. We recover the absolute query pose from the ground-truth poses of the retrieved frames and their predicted poses in the map. We report the median translation and rotation errors and the recall within 5 cm and 5 for 7-Scenes [71] and within 25 cm and 2 for Cambridge [43]. All methods attend to the same map frames. We time each query on one H100 GPU, from encoding the query to reading out its pose, including copy17 ing the cached key-value pairs of its retrieved frames from host memory. Streaming reconstruction. We evaluate on Sintel [13], TUM dynamics [73], ScanNet [23], Bonn [64], KITTI [33], 7-Scenes [71], and NRGBD [3]. We use 1000 frames with stride of 3 for ScanNet, 500 frames for Bonn and KITTI, and 200 frames with stride of 2 for 7-Scenes and NRGBD. We evaluate each frame with its prediction at arrival, before any later refinement. The first eight frames are an exception, since Solv3R solves them jointly as anchors. We report the absolute trajectory error (ATE) after Sim(3) alignment [81], the depth AbsRel and δ1.25 after per-sequence scale alignment, and the Chamfer distance and normal consistency of the reconstructed point clouds.
